title: CUET Political Science Test 6
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Political Science papers 2024 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: President who proclaimed the Emergency
questions.question: Who was the President of India when the Emergency was proclaimed in June 1975?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
Why: President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed the Emergency on the advice of the Prime Minister.
Why not the others:
(B) Giri's term ended in 1974.
(C) Zakir Hussain died in office in 1969.
(D) Sanjiva Reddy became President in 1977.
Key point: The Cabinet was told only after the proclamation.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Number of UN member states
questions.question: How many member states does the United Nations have today?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 193
Why: The UN now has 193 member states.
Why not the others:
(A) 51 states founded the UN.
(B), (D) These figures are not the UN's membership.
Key point: The UN has grown from 51 to 193 members.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Movements in the South, Assam and Goa — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Dravidian movement was led by E.V. Ramasami Naicker, 'Periyar'.
(B) Tamil Nadu saw an anti-Hindi agitation in 1965.
(C) The Assam movement against 'outsiders' ran from 1979 to 1985.
(D) Goa was freed from French rule in 1961.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) Periyar led the Dravidian movement. (B) there was a major anti-Hindi agitation in 1965. (C) the Assam movement lasted from 1979 to 1985.
Why not the others: (D) is false: Goa was freed from Portuguese rule in 1961. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (B).
Key point: Regional movements took many forms.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Political terms from 1967 to 1971
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Defection
(B) Coalition
(C) Non-Congressism
(D) Conscience vote

List-II
(I) A strategy of uniting the opposition against the Congress
(II) Indira Gandhi's call to Congress legislators to vote freely in the 1969 presidential election
(III) A legislator leaving the party on whose ticket he or she was elected
(IV) An alliance of parties to form a government
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Defection means leaving one's party (III). A coalition is an alliance to form a government (IV). Non-Congressism united the opposition (I). The conscience vote was Indira Gandhi's call in 1969 (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps defection and coalition. Option (B) swaps coalition and non-Congressism. Option (C) swaps non-Congressism and the conscience vote.
Key point: These terms describe the politics that broke the Congress system.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Genocide the world failed to prevent
questions.question: In 1994 a genocide in which about half a million people were killed in a few weeks took place in which country, while the international community failed to act?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Rwanda
Why: NCERT cites the Rwandan genocide of 1994 as a failure of the international community to protect people.
Why not the others: (A), (C), (D) Each saw conflict, but the 1994 genocide was in Rwanda.
Key point: Human security asks whether the world will protect people from mass killing.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: An example of outsourcing
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of outsourcing linked with globalisation?
options: A) Foreign companies using call centres in India
B) A farmer selling grain in the local market
C) A State government building a road
D) A village panchayat collecting taxes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Foreign companies using call centres in India
Why: Foreign firms hiring call centres in India to serve their customers is outsourcing.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) These are local activities with no cross-border flow.
Key point: Information technology made outsourcing possible.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Who led the armed insurgency in Nepal
questions.question: The armed insurgency in Nepal from the mid-1990s was led by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) the Maoists
Why: The Maoists led an armed struggle against the monarchy and the ruling elite, and later joined the democratic process.
Why not the others:
(B) The army fought the insurgents.
(C) The king's supporters opposed the Maoists.
(D) The Nepali Congress was a mainstream party.
Key point: The Maoist insurgency shaped Nepal's move to a republic.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Prime Minister for thirteen days in 1996
questions.question: Who became Prime Minister in 1996 but resigned after about thirteen days because he could not win a majority?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Atal Bihari Vajpayee
Why: Vajpayee formed a government in May 1996 as leader of the largest party, but resigned within thirteen days.
Why not the others:
(A) Deve Gowda then led the United Front.
(C) Gujral followed in 1997.
(D) V.P. Singh was Prime Minister in 1989–90.
Key point: Being the largest party was not enough to rule.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Dimensions of globalisation and examples
questions.question:
Match List-I (Aspect) with List-II (Example).

List-I
(A) Economic globalisation
(B) Political globalisation
(C) Cultural globalisation
(D) Technology

List-II
(I) The internet and telecommunications speed up flows
(II) Greater trade and investment across borders
(III) A shrinking welfare role for the state
(IV) The spread of Western food, dress and music
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: Economic globalisation means more trade and investment (II). Political globalisation can shrink the welfare state (III). Cultural globalisation spreads Western food, dress and music (IV). Technology speeds up all these flows (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the economic and political aspects. Option (B) swaps the political and cultural aspects. Option (D) swaps cultural globalisation and technology.
Key point: Globalisation is economic, political and cultural, driven by technology.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Architect of India's early foreign policy
questions.question: Who served as both Prime Minister and Foreign Minister and shaped India's foreign policy from 1947 to 1964?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Jawaharlal Nehru
Why: Nehru held the external affairs portfolio along with the prime ministership and was the main architect of India's foreign policy.
Why not the others:
(A) Patel was Home Minister.
(C) Krishna Menon was Defence Minister in 1962.
(D) Shastri became Prime Minister only in 1964.
Key point: Nehru's ideas of non-alignment and peace shaped India's early diplomacy.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Princely state whose ruler first announced independence
questions.question: Which of the following princely states had a ruler who at first refused to join India and announced that the State would stay independent?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Travancore
Why: The ruler of Travancore, like those of Hyderabad, Kashmir and Bhopal, at first refused to join India.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (C) Bhavnagar, Jaisalmer and Gwalior joined without such resistance.
Key point: Most rulers signed the Instrument of Accession; a few held out.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Which is NOT a permanent member of the Security Council
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a permanent member of the UN Security Council?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Germany
Why: Germany is not a permanent member, though it seeks a seat in a reformed Council.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) China, France and Russia are permanent members, along with the UK and the USA.
Key point: The permanent five reflect the world of 1945.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Terms from land and agricultural policy
questions.question:
Match List-I (Policy) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Land ceiling
(B) Green Revolution
(C) Operation Flood
(D) Abolition of zamindari

List-II
(I) High-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation to raise food output
(II) A limit on the amount of land one person can own
(III) Ending the system of landlords who stood between farmers and the state
(IV) A programme of milk cooperatives to raise dairy production
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: A land ceiling limits how much land one person can own (II). The Green Revolution used high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation (I). Operation Flood organised milk cooperatives (IV). Abolishing zamindari ended the landlord system (III).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps the ceiling and the Green Revolution. Option (C) swaps the Green Revolution and Operation Flood. Option (D) swaps Operation Flood and zamindari abolition.
Key point: Land reform and new technology both aimed to transform farming.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Country whose example inspired India's Five Year Plans
questions.question: India's idea of Five Year Plans drew on the example of which country?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The Soviet Union
Why: The Soviet Union's Five Year Plans inspired India's model of planning, though India kept a mixed economy.
Why not the others: (A), (C), (D) These countries did not use Five Year Plans as the base of their economies.
Key point: India borrowed planning, not the whole Soviet system.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Organisations banned during the Emergency
questions.question: Which organisations were banned during the Emergency?
options: A) The Swatantra Party and the Socialist Party
B) The CPI and the DMK
C) The Akali Dal and the Republican Party
D) The RSS and the Jamaat-e-Islami
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The RSS and the Jamaat-e-Islami
Why: The government banned the RSS and the Jamaat-e-Islami, among others.
Why not the others:
(A) These parties were not banned in this way.
(B) The CPI supported the Emergency.
(C) These were not the organisations banned.
Key point: The Emergency curbed organisations as well as the press.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Which is NOT an argument of globalisation's critics
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an argument made by critics of globalisation?
options: A) It makes the rich richer and the poor poorer.
B) It weakens the state's ability to protect its poor.
D) It always reduces poverty in every country.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It always reduces poverty in every country.
Why: Claiming that globalisation always reduces poverty is the opposite of what critics argue.
Why not the others:
(A) Critics on the left argue it increases inequality.
(B) They argue it weakens the welfare state.
(C) Critics on the right fear cultural loss.
Key point: Critics come from both the left and the right.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Island country south-west of India
questions.question: Which SAARC member is a country of islands in the Indian Ocean, south-west of India?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Maldives
Why: The Maldives is a group of islands south-west of India.
Why not the others:
(A) Sri Lanka is an island to the south-east of India.
(C), (D) Bhutan and Nepal are landlocked.
Key point: South Asia includes both Himalayan and island states.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Jammu and Kashmir, 1953–2019, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) The special status under Article 370 is ended
(B) Sheikh Abdullah is dismissed as Prime Minister of the State
(C) Militancy takes hold in the Kashmir valley
(D) Indira Gandhi and Sheikh Abdullah reach an agreement
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (D), (C), (A)
Why: (B) Sheikh Abdullah was dismissed in 1953. (D) The agreement with Indira Gandhi came in 1974. (C) Militancy took hold from 1989. (A) Article 370 was ended in 2019.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts militancy before the 1974 agreement. Option (B) puts 1974 before 1953. Option (D) puts 2019 before 1989.
Key point: 1953 → 1974 → 1989 → 2019.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Country used to contrast with the Congress's dominance
questions.question: NCERT contrasts the Congress's dominance, which existed alongside free elections, with one-party rule in a country where the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) ruled for about sixty years. Which country was it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mexico
Why: The PRI ruled Mexico for about sixty years, but without the free competition that India's democracy allowed.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) NCERT's example is Mexico.
Key point: India's one-party dominance was democratic.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Full form of OBC
questions.question: What does 'OBC' stand for?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Other Backward Classes
Why: OBC stands for Other Backward Classes.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) are not the official term.
Key point: OBC reservation in central jobs followed the Mandal Commission.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: The Soviet system — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Soviet Union came into being after the socialist revolution of 1917.
(B) The Soviet system became very bureaucratic and authoritarian.
(C) Soviet citizens enjoyed a higher standard of living than people in Western Europe.
(D) The Communist Party dominated all institutions.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the Soviet Union fell behind the West in technology, consumer goods and living standards.
Why not the others: (A) the USSR emerged from the 1917 revolution. (B) the system was bureaucratic and authoritarian. (D) the Communist Party controlled every institution. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The gap with the West made Soviet citizens restless.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Starting point of the 1990 rath yatra
questions.question: In 1990 the BJP organised a march called the Rath Yatra to Ayodhya. Where did it start?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Somnath
Why: The Rath Yatra started from Somnath in Gujarat and was meant to end at Ayodhya.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (C) None of these was the starting point.
Key point: The Ayodhya issue became central to national politics in the early 1990s.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: The end of the Soviet bloc in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) Communist hardliners attempt a coup against Gorbachev
(B) Boris Yeltsin is elected President of Russia
(C) The Berlin Wall falls
(D) The Soviet Union is dissolved
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C), (B), (A), (D)
Why: (C) The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989. (B) Yeltsin was elected President of Russia in June 1991. (A) The hardliners' coup failed in August 1991. (D) The Soviet Union was dissolved in December 1991.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the coup before Yeltsin's election. Option (C) puts 1991 before 1989. Option (D) puts the dissolution before the coup.
Key point: 1989 → June 1991 → August 1991 → December 1991.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: India and its neighbours — points of contact
questions.question:
Match List-I (Neighbour) with List-II (Point of cooperation or friction with India).

List-I
(A) Nepal
(B) Maldives
(C) Sri Lanka
(D) Bangladesh

List-II
(I) Illegal migration has been a point of friction
(II) A treaty lets citizens travel and work in each other's country without visas
(III) India sent help after the 2004 tsunami
(IV) India helped foil a coup attempt in 1988
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: India and Nepal have an open-border treaty (II). India helped the Maldives foil a coup attempt in 1988 (IV). India helped Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami (III). Illegal migration is a point of friction with Bangladesh (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Nepal and the Maldives. Option (B) swaps the Maldives and Sri Lanka. Option (D) swaps Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
Key point: India's ties with each neighbour mix cooperation and friction.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Size of the electorate in the first general election
questions.question: About how many voters were eligible to vote in India's first general election?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 17 crore
Why: About 17 crore people were eligible to vote, most of whom could not read or write.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (D) These figures do not match the first electorate.
Key point: India's first election was the largest democratic exercise of its time.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: India's external relations, 1954–1971, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) The first NAM summit at Belgrade
(B) The Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace and Friendship
(C) The Panchsheel agreement with China
(D) The Dalai Lama is given asylum in India
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: (C) Panchsheel was signed in 1954. (D) The Dalai Lama came to India in 1959. (A) The Belgrade summit met in 1961. (B) The Indo-Soviet Treaty was signed in 1971.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Belgrade before the Dalai Lama's arrival. Option (B) puts 1959 before 1954. Option (C) puts the 1971 treaty before Belgrade.
Key point: 1954 → 1959 → 1961 → 1971.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Why fresh water can cause conflict between countries
questions.question: Why can fresh water become a cause of conflict between countries?
options: A) Because the United Nations owns and manages most of the world's major rivers
B) Because rivers often cross borders, so upstream use affects downstream states
C) Because fresh water is found only in a handful of desert countries of West Asia
D) Because the WTO fixes the international prices of all water exports
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Because rivers often cross borders, so upstream use affects downstream states
Why: Rivers shared by several countries create disputes when upstream states dam or divert water.
Why not the others:
(A) The UN does not own rivers.
(C) Fresh water is found across the world.
(D) The WTO does not set water prices.
Key point: Water scarcity can lead to 'water wars'.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Year of Pakistan's nuclear tests
questions.question: In which year did Pakistan carry out its nuclear tests, soon after India's?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1998
Why: Pakistan tested nuclear devices in May 1998, weeks after India's tests.
Why not the others:
(A) 1974 was India's first test.
(B) 1971 was the Bangladesh war.
(C) 1999 was the year of Kargil.
Key point: Both countries became declared nuclear powers in 1998.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: An epidemic named as a security threat
questions.question: Which of the following is an epidemic NCERT names among the threats to human security that spread across borders?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) SARS
Why: SARS, like HIV-AIDS and bird flu, is an epidemic that spread across borders and threatened human security.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (D) These are environmental problems, not epidemics.
Key point: Disease is a non-traditional security threat.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: What happened to former communist states
questions.question:
Match List-I (Country or group) with List-II (What happened after communism).

List-I
(A) Czechoslovakia
(B) Germany
(C) Yugoslavia
(D) The Baltic states

List-II
(I) Broke apart amid violent ethnic conflict
(II) The East and the West were unified
(III) Joined both the EU and NATO
(IV) Split peacefully into two countries
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia (IV). Germany was unified in 1990 (II). Yugoslavia broke apart in violence (I). The Baltic states joined the EU and NATO (III).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Czechoslovakia and Germany. Option (C) swaps Germany and Yugoslavia. Option (D) swaps Yugoslavia and the Baltic states.
Key point: The end of communism took very different paths.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Nehru's successor as Prime Minister
questions.question: Who succeeded Jawaharlal Nehru as Prime Minister in 1964?
options: D) Gulzarilal Nanda as an elected Prime Minister
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Lal Bahadur Shastri
Why: Lal Bahadur Shastri became Prime Minister after Nehru's death in 1964.
Why not the others:
(B) Indira Gandhi became Prime Minister in 1966.
(C) Morarji Desai became Prime Minister in 1977.
(D) Nanda was only an interim Prime Minister.
Key point: The first succession after Nehru was peaceful.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Linguistic reorganisation of States in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Maharashtra and Gujarat are formed
(B) The Andhra State is formed
(C) Punjab and Haryana are created
(D) The States Reorganisation Act is passed
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: (B) Andhra was formed in 1953. (D) The States Reorganisation Act was passed in 1956. (A) Bombay State was divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat in 1960. (C) Punjab and Haryana were created in 1966.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts 1960 before 1956. Option (C) puts the Act before Andhra. Option (D) puts 1966 before 1960.
Key point: 1953 → 1956 → 1960 → 1966.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Body to which India took the Kashmir issue in 1948
questions.question: In 1948, India took the issue of Pakistan-backed raiders in Kashmir to:
options: D) the International Court of Justice
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) the United Nations
Why: India referred the Kashmir issue to the United Nations in 1948.
Why not the others:
(A) The Commonwealth was not asked to decide it.
(B) NAM did not exist until 1961.
(D) The ICJ was not approached.
Key point: The Kashmir issue has remained an India–Pakistan dispute since 1948.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Party that came to power after the Assam Accord
questions.question: After the Assam Accord, which party, formed by the leaders of the Assam movement, won the 1985 State elections?
options: B) United Liberation Front of Asom
D) Assam Gana Sangram Parishad of Nagaland
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Asom Gana Parishad
Why: The Asom Gana Parishad, formed by leaders of the movement, won the 1985 elections.
Why not the others:
(B) ULFA was an armed separatist group.
(C) The MNF was based in Mizoram.
(D) No such Nagaland party existed.
Key point: Movement leaders entered electoral politics.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: How the UN works — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In the General Assembly, every member state has one vote.
(B) The Secretary-General is appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council.
(C) The five permanent members of the Security Council have a veto.
(D) India has never been elected a non-permanent member of the Security Council.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) each member has one vote in the General Assembly. (B) the Secretary-General is appointed on the Security Council's recommendation. (C) each permanent member has a veto.
Why not the others: (D) is false: India has been elected a non-permanent member several times. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: The General Assembly is equal; the Security Council is not.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: The state of the global environment — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The ozone hole was first found over the Arctic.
(B) Many grasslands have been overgrazed and fisheries overharvested.
(C) Coastal pollution is increasing.
(D) About 1.2 billion people in developing countries lack access to safe water.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: the ozone hole was found over the Antarctic.
Why not the others: (B) NCERT notes overgrazed grasslands and overharvested fisheries. (C) coastal pollution is rising. (D) about 1.2 billion people lack safe water. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Environmental damage is global and uneven.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Main gas behind global warming
questions.question: Global warming is mainly caused by the build-up of greenhouse gases. Which is the most important of these?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Carbon dioxide
Why: Carbon dioxide, released mostly by burning fossil fuels, is the main greenhouse gas.
Why not the others:
(A) Sulphur dioxide is linked mainly with acid rain.
(B), (C) Nitrogen, argon and helium do not trap heat in this way.
Key point: Cutting carbon emissions is central to climate negotiations.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: BJP's Lok Sabha tally in four elections
questions.question:
Match List-I (Lok Sabha election) with List-II (Seats won by the BJP).

List-I
(A) 1989
(B) 1991
(C) 1998
(D) 2014

List-II
(I) 182
(II) 85
(III) 282
(IV) 120
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: The BJP won 85 seats in 1989 (II), 120 in 1991 (IV), 182 in 1998 (I) and 282 in 2014 (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps 1989 and 1991. Option (B) swaps 1991 and 1998. Option (C) swaps 1998 and 2014.
Key point: The BJP rose from a small party to a majority on its own.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Weapons of mass destruction
questions.question: Which of the following are counted as weapons of mass destruction?
options: A) Tanks, missiles and fighter aircraft
D) Nuclear, biological and chemical weapons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Nuclear, biological and chemical weapons
Why: Nuclear, biological and chemical weapons can kill on a massive scale, and are called weapons of mass destruction.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (C) These are conventional weapons.
Key point: Arms-control treaties target weapons of mass destruction.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Programme adopted by the Congress in 1967
questions.question: In 1967 the Congress Working Committee adopted a programme that included social control of banks, nationalisation of general insurance and land reforms. What was it called?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The Ten Point Programme
Why: The Ten Point Programme of 1967 gave the Congress a more left-leaning agenda.
Why not the others:
(A) The Twenty Point Programme came during the Emergency.
(B) The Bombay Plan was drafted by industrialists in 1944.
(D) There was no such charter.
Key point: The Ten Point Programme foreshadowed bank nationalisation.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Provision used to dismiss Kerala's government in 1959
questions.question: In 1959 the Congress government at the Centre dismissed the Communist government of Kerala. Which provision of the Constitution did it use?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Article 356
Why: The Kerala government was dismissed under Article 356, which allows President's Rule in a State.
Why not the others:
(A) Article 352 deals with a national emergency.
(B) Article 360 deals with a financial emergency.
(C) Article 370 concerned Jammu and Kashmir.
Key point: The use of Article 356 against Kerala became a controversial precedent.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: India's energy links with post-Soviet states
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of India's energy cooperation with the post-Soviet states?
options: A) A complete Indian ban on all oil imports from Central Asia
B) A joint army command set up by India and Russia in 1992
C) Russia's full membership of SAARC since its founding
D) Indian investment in oil fields in Russia and Kazakhstan
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Indian investment in oil fields in Russia and Kazakhstan
Why: India has invested in oil fields in Russia and Kazakhstan as part of its search for energy security.
Why not the others:
(A) There is no such ban.
(B) India and Russia have no joint army command.
(C) Russia is not a member of SAARC.
Key point: Energy is a key part of India's ties with Russia and Central Asia.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Rules of the Emergency — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The 1975 Emergency was declared on the ground of internal disturbance.
(B) Indira Gandhi called the 1977 elections because the Supreme Court ordered her to.
(C) The 44th Amendment later replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground for an emergency.
(D) During the Emergency, citizens' right to move the courts to enforce Fundamental Rights could be suspended.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: Indira Gandhi announced the 1977 elections herself; no court ordered her to.
Why not the others: (A) the Emergency was declared on the ground of internal disturbance. (C) the 44th Amendment of 1978 made armed rebellion the ground. (D) the right to move the courts could be suspended. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The Emergency led to safeguards against its misuse.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Challenges of nation-building — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Independent India faced three main challenges: unity, democracy and development.
(B) Potti Sriramulu died after a fast of 56 days for an Andhra State.
(C) Partition meant dividing government assets, from money and railways to office furniture.
(D) Nehru supported the creation of linguistic States immediately after Independence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) NCERT names unity, democracy and development as the three challenges. (B) Sriramulu died after a 56-day fast in 1952. (C) Partition required the division of all kinds of property.
Why not the others: (D) is false: Nehru and others were wary of linguistic States after Partition. Options (B) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Nation-building began with three challenges at once.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Outside support for the United Front government
questions.question: The United Front government of 1996 survived with outside support from:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) the Congress
Why: The Congress backed the United Front from outside to keep the BJP out of power.
Why not the others:
(A) The BJP was the main opposition.
(B) The Shiv Sena was a BJP ally.
(D) The AGP was itself a part of the United Front.
Key point: Outside support made coalition governments fragile.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Source of the aid that revived Western Europe
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

When the Second World War ended, the economies of Western Europe lay in ruins. The United States helped them recover through a large programme of aid known as the Marshall Plan, and in 1948 the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation was set up to channel this aid to the Western European states. In 1949 the Council of Europe was formed to promote political cooperation. Step by step, economic integration deepened, from a common market to a European Union with its own flag, anthem, founding date and currency. Not every member wanted to go so far: some, such as Denmark and Sweden, resisted the move to a single currency and kept their own. Economically the Union is a giant. Its share of world trade is far larger than that of the United States, and its currency, the euro, could one day challenge the dominance of the US dollar. It carries political and diplomatic weight too. France is a nuclear power and a permanent member of the UN Security Council, and the Union's combined armed forces are among the largest in the world. Yet the EU is not a single state. Its members keep their own foreign and defence policies and often disagree. When the United States invaded Iraq in 2003, some members joined the war while Germany and France opposed it.

Question: According to the passage, the Marshall Plan, which helped Western Europe recover after the war, was a programme of aid from:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) the United States
Why: The passage says the United States helped Western Europe recover through the Marshall Plan.
Why not the others:
(A) The Soviet Union led the rival bloc.
(C) The passage does not link the plan to the UN.
(D) The Council of Europe was formed later, for political cooperation.
Key point: American aid laid the base for European integration.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Why the OEEC was set up in 1948
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: According to the passage, why was the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation set up in 1948?
options: A) To channel Marshall Plan aid to the Western European states
B) To create a single European currency at once
C) To form a military alliance against the Soviet Union
D) To settle border disputes between France and Germany
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) To channel Marshall Plan aid to the Western European states
Why: The passage says the OEEC was set up in 1948 to channel the American aid to Western Europe.
Why not the others:
(B) A single currency came decades later.
(C) The passage does not describe the OEEC as a military alliance.
(D) Border disputes are not mentioned.
Key point: The OEEC became a forum for European economic cooperation.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Body formed in 1949 for political cooperation

Question: Which body, according to the passage, was formed in 1949 to promote political cooperation in Europe?
options: B) The Organisation for European Economic Cooperation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The Council of Europe
Why: The passage says the Council of Europe was formed in 1949 to promote political cooperation.
Why not the others:
(A) The EEC was an economic body formed later.
(B) The OEEC, formed in 1948, dealt with economic aid.
(C) The passage does not mention a central bank.
Key point: Political cooperation grew alongside economic integration.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Which claim about the EU is NOT supported
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage?
options: A) The EU's share of world trade is larger than that of the United States.
B) EU members keep their own foreign and defence policies.
C) Every member of the EU has adopted the euro.
D) EU members disagreed over the invasion of Iraq in 2003.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Every member of the EU has adopted the euro.
Why: The passage says some members, such as Denmark and Sweden, resisted the single currency and kept their own.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage says the EU's share of world trade is far larger.
(B) It says members keep their own foreign and defence policies.
(D) It says some joined the Iraq war while Germany and France opposed it.
Key point: Integration in the EU is deep but not uniform.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: What the passage suggests about the EU's influence
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

When the Second World War ended, the economies of Western Europe lay in ruins. The United States helped them recover through a large programme of aid known as the Marshall Plan, and in 1948 the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation was set up to channel this aid to the Western European states. Yet the EU is not a single state. Its members keep their own foreign and defence policies and often disagree. When the United States invaded Iraq in 2003, some members joined the war while Germany and France opposed it.

Question: What can best be inferred from the passage about the European Union's influence in world affairs?
options: A) The EU matters in world affairs only because of its large armed forces.
B) Its influence rests on economic, political and diplomatic strength together.
C) The EU has no real influence, because its members sometimes disagree.
D) The EU's influence depends entirely on its close alliance with the United States.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Its influence rests on economic, political and diplomatic strength together.
Why: The passage stresses the EU's economic size, its diplomatic weight through France's seat on the Security Council, and its large combined forces.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage puts economic strength first.
(C) Disagreement limits, but does not remove, its influence.
(D) The passage shows the EU differing from the United States, for example over Iraq.
Key point: The EU is an economic, political and diplomatic power.
